what: Three answers of shared/taskAssignment.ts that move into the core: the new assignee list a status change implies (self-assign on start or finish, step back on reopen), how many people a list can hold on one task, and what a list of assignees is trimmed to. Measured from the TypeScript before the port. The fourth rule of the module, "is this mine?", is already the core’s and has its own contract (shared/contracts/taskOwnership.json).
why: Both surfaces apply these when a task is checked off or moved, and a frontend that is not JavaScript has to apply them too. The core answers WHO by position (which of the given assignees stay) or by a state (take me), never by echoing a user row; the mode and the trim are what stop an editor from offering a choice the source cannot keep.
writtenBy: src/state/taskAssignment.measure.test.ts — a one-off, run once and deleted; its cases mirror src/state/taskAssignment.test.ts plus the rows the port needs that those never had (order kept when I am in the middle, every copy of me removed, cancelling a task I hold, in_progress on a colleague’s task, an empty list under single, every declared mode).

whereItLives.note: Inside cal-core, like the other task fixtures; taskOwnership.json stays in shared/contracts/ because host-core reads it and host-core never leaves this repository.

notInThisTable.isMineOrUnassigned: already the core’s (cal_core::is_mine_or_unassigned), pinned by shared/contracts/taskOwnership.json; its last TypeScript copy went when the day-start rules moved into the core (cal_core::day_start)
notInThisTable.classifyDoneByMe: no caller since the grouping moved into the core (#42); deleted with the port
notInThisTable.currentUserForList: who "me" is for a list is the platform’s (a session-cached adapter call); the rule takes it as an input
notInThisTable.the Settings toggle: whether the auto-assign is on travels in as `enabled`

shape.selfAssign: {nextStatus, assignees: [id…], me: id | null, enabled} → the new assignee ids or null (nothing changes). A user is its id: the rule compares ids alone.
shape.clamp: {mode, assignees: [id…]} → the ids that stay, in order.

selfAssign.name: an-unassigned-task-going-in-progress-becomes-mine
selfAssign.note: The auto-assign: work started on a task nobody owns.

selfAssign.name: an-unassigned-task-completed-becomes-mine
selfAssign.note: Finishing it counts as taking it.

selfAssign.name: a-task-a-colleague-holds-is-not-taken
selfAssign.note: The auto-assign acts only on a task nobody owns.

selfAssign.name: reopening-removes-only-me
selfAssign.note: Symmetric to the auto-assign: I step back, nobody else is touched.

selfAssign.name: reopening-keeps-the-colleague-in-order
selfAssign.note: The remaining assignees keep their order.

selfAssign.name: reopening-removes-every-copy-of-me
selfAssign.note: A provider that lists the same person twice loses both copies; matching is by id.

selfAssign.name: cancelling-changes-nothing
selfAssign.note: Cancelled is neither taking nor stepping back.

selfAssign.name: no-identity-changes-nothing
selfAssign.note: A list whose adapter reports no "me" (the local store) has nobody to assign.

selfAssign.name: in-progress-with-a-colleague-is-left-alone
selfAssign.note: Starting work on a task someone else holds does not add me.

mode.name: a-capabilities-block-without-the-field-cannot-assign
mode.note: An adapter that has not said it can assign is taken at its word.

clamp.name: single-keeps-the-first
clamp.note: The same one Todoist’s adapter keeps (first_assignee_id), so the editor and the wire agree about who survives.

clamp.name: none-never-empties-what-it-cannot-show
clamp.note: The editor hides the picker there; the task may still carry assignees another client wrote, and clearing them on open would destroy what the user was never shown.
